Let c = P(0) and write P(x) = c + x·Q(x), where Q has integer coefficients (this holds for any integer-coefficient polynomial). The conditions become:

- Q(−10) = (c − 145)/10 must be an integer.
- Q(9) = (164 − c)/9 must be an integer.

An integer-coefficient polynomial Q exists with prescribed integer values at −10 and 9 exactly when 9 − (−10) = 19 divides the difference of those values. Here this difference is

Q(9) − Q(−10) = (164 − c)/9 + (145 − c)/10 = (2945 − 19c)/90 = 19(155 − c)/90.

Since 19 is coprime to 90, this is divisible by 19 only if (155 − c)/90 is an integer. That gives c ≡ 155 ≡ 65 (mod 90).

This congruence already implies both integrality conditions (c ≡ 5 mod 10 and c ≡ 2 mod 9), and the conditions are also sufficient. We can interpolate a suitable Q and then set P(x) = c + x·Q(x).

The values c ≡ 65 (mod 90) near zero are −25, 65, −115, …. The smallest absolute value is |−25| = 25.

ANSWER: 25
